frontmatter.title: Responses to Events and Placement Duration

children.value: This chapter describes what participants did on the first two placements after a single displaced attack (an oddball or the first attack of a new episode), and how long they took to place the nets on these trials. Both are reported by instruction condition and by questionnaire score. The analyses of net placement error (Model B1) and net entropy (Model B2) after events in
Results by Research Question
, section 2.2, describe the same trials by continuous measures; the strategies below decompose these measures into the discrete placements that produce them.
Classification of the placements after events

children.label: Classification of the placements after events

children.value: Each placement at t+1 and t+2 was classified relative to the participant’s own placement on the event trial (t0), not relative to the hidden-state target, because participants in None and Partial were often far from the target before the event, so that a classification by target directions assigns many placements to none of the categories. Three anchors were defined for each event, the centre of the allocation at t0 (old direction), the direction 120° from it toward the displaced attack (new direction) and the direction 120° from it on the other side (third direction). For placements of the second color cue, the allocation was first rotated by the cue offset the participant had learned, so that both cues are expressed in the frame of the first. The share of the seven nets within two positions (±22.5°) of each anchor and the shift of the allocation centre from t0 defined six classes, assigned in the order nets on both directions (at least a quarter of the nets at the old and at the new direction), followed (at least half at the new direction, or a shift of at least 90° toward the attack), stayed (at least half at the old direction, or a shift of less than 30°), moved the other way (at least half at the third direction, or a shift of at least 90° away from the attack), moved part of the way (a shift between 30° and 90° toward the attack) and spread (all remaining placements). The classes refer to the location of the nets and not to the participant’s intention; a placement with all nets at the new direction after an oddball is classified as followed, although following an oddball is not adaptive.

The analysis comprised 2,030 events (1,345 oddballs and 685 transitions) of 86 participants. The probability of each class was modelled with logistic generalized estimating equations (GEE) clustered by participant with an exchangeable working correlation, with the planned condition contrasts (Benjamini–Hochberg correction across the strategies), and, for the questionnaires, with the standardized questionnaire score and condition as predictors, in an across-condition form and a form with the Full × questionnaire interaction (Benjamini–Hochberg correction across the five core questionnaires per strategy and term; the five further questionnaires of the battery were corrected separately and are not reported here). Two participant-level measures summarize the distinction between the events, the selectivity at t+1 (share of transitions followed minus share of oddballs followed) and the selectivity at t+2 (share of transitions at the new direction minus share of oddballs at the new direction), together with the share of correct placements at t+2 (at the new direction after transitions, at the t0 placement after oddballs); these were modelled with linear regressions with heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors. The statistics of this analysis are computed in Python (
tambi_event_strategies.py
); moving them to R mixed models is an open item.
Strategies at t+1

After transitions, participants told the structure followed the displaced attack on the first placement significantly more often than participants not told it (shares of transitions followed, None .27, Partial .28, Full .47; planned contrast Full versus None and Partial = 0.86 log-odds, p = .001, q = .004), and the share did not differ between Partial and None (0.02, p = .95). After oddballs, participants told the structure stayed at their t0 placement significantly more often (None .32, Partial .35, Full .52; planned contrast = 0.78 log-odds, p < .001, q < .001), whereas the share of oddballs followed did not differ between conditions (None .24, Partial .21, Full .22; planned contrast = −0.05, p = .82). Moving part of the way after oddballs (None .10, Partial .14, Full .06; −0.86, p = .003, q = .008) and spread placements after both events (transitions, None .08, Partial .06, Full .01, −1.86, p = .009, q = .022; oddballs, None .13, Partial .09, Full .04, −1.12, p = .003, q = .008) were significantly less frequent in Full. Nets on both directions occurred after 12 % to 14 % of transitions and 6 % to 10 % of oddballs, without a significant difference between conditions (all p ≥ .20).

The selectivity at t+1 was significantly larger in Full than in None and Partial (mean selectivity, None 0.03, Partial 0.06, Full 0.25; planned contrast = 0.21, p = .001, q = .004). Participants not told the structure thus followed a displaced attack on the first placement with nearly the same probability whether it was an oddball or the first attack of a new episode, whereas participants told the structure followed transitions about twice as often as oddballs, although the two events present the same evidence at this point (

Strategies at t+2

On the second placement after transitions, the share of placements at the new direction was significantly higher in Full (None .41, Partial .38, Full .67; planned contrast = 1.15 log-odds, p < .001), and so was the share of placements back at the t0 placement after oddballs (None .39, Partial .43, Full .68; 1.10, p < .001). Participants told the structure kept the new direction at t+2 after following a transition at t+1 more often (None .58, Partial .62, Full .90; 1.79, p < .001), moved to it at t+2 more often when they had not followed at t+1 (None .34, Partial .29, Full .46; 0.63, p = .015, q = .035), and returned to the t0 placement more often after moving toward an oddball at t+1 (None .31, Partial .38, Full .57; 0.91, p = .001, q = .004). The share of correct placements at t+2 was .39 (None), .41 (Partial) and .67 (Full) (planned contrast = 0.27, p < .001), and the selectivity at t+2 was 0.21, 0.23 and 0.56 (0.34, p < .001). No contrast between Partial and None was significant for any strategy at t+1 or t+2 (all q ≥ .70).

Questionnaire scores and strategies

Higher STICSA state anxiety and BDI scores were significantly associated with following transitions less often at t+1 (STICSA state, −0.30 log-odds per SD, p = .008, q = .041; BDI, −0.27, p = .016, q = .041), and STICSA trait anxiety showed the same direction at the threshold of the correction (−0.24, p = .032, q = .054); the association did not depend on instruction (Full × questionnaire, all p ≥ .31). The share of oddballs followed at t+1 was not associated with any of the five questionnaires (coefficients between −0.07 and 0.05). Accordingly, the selectivity at t+1 was significantly lower with higher STICSA state (−0.059 per SD, p = .005, q = .026), STICSA trait (−0.051, p = .012, q = .029) and BDI scores (−0.053, p = .019, q = .031). For scale, the mean selectivity in None and Partial was 0.03 and 0.06, and the difference between Full and the other two conditions 0.21, so that one SD on these questionnaires corresponds to about a quarter of the instruction effect.

Higher BDI scores were significantly associated with nets on both directions at t+1 after transitions (0.33, p = .002, q = .008) and after both events together (0.26, p = .006, q = .032). At t+2 after transitions, nets on both directions were significantly more frequent with higher STICSA state anxiety (0.46, p < .001, q = .002), STICSA trait anxiety (0.33, p = .025, q = .031), BDI (0.36, p = .006, q = .010) and OCI scores (0.39, p = .006, q = .010); at t+2 after oddballs, they were more frequent with higher STICSA state anxiety (0.38, p = .001, q = .005). With windows of ±1 instead of ±2 positions around the anchors, the associations at t+2 were weaker, and the association of STICSA state anxiety was retained with a measure that requires no threshold (share of the nets on the less covered of the two directions; p ≤ .014). The share of placements at the new direction at t+2 after transitions, the share back at the t0 placement after oddballs and the share of correct placements at t+2 were not associated with any questionnaire. Among the transitions followed at t+1, higher IU (0.49, p = .004, q = .020) and OCI scores (0.43, p = .008, q = .020) were associated with keeping the new direction at t+2.

Participants with higher state anxiety, trait anxiety and depression scores thus followed a transition less often on the first placement, without following oddballs less often, and placed nets on both directions more often on the first and second placement. By the second placement, they were as often at the new direction after transitions and back at the old direction after oddballs as participants with lower scores. The strategies therefore show which placements underlie the higher net placement error at t+1 after transitions (Model B1) and the wider allocation after events (Model B2) in the results by research question.
Placement duration at t0, t+1 and t+2

children.label: Placement duration at t0, t+1 and t+2

children.value: The placement duration is the time from the start of the placement phase until all seven nets are placed, or 7 s if they are not (4.7 % of trials). It was modelled on the log scale with a linear mixed model of condition × event type × trial (t0, t+1, t+2) with the trial index of the session as covariate and random effects for participants (intercept and trial) and for events within participants (
tambi_placement_duration.R

, P0). Two sensitivity models added the number of positions used and the log of the shift of the allocation centre (P0_adj), which index the amount of placement work, or excluded the time-outs. Estimates are given in log units, which for differences of this size correspond approximately to proportional changes (0.04 ≈ 4 %).

The median placement duration was 4.1 to 4.4 s at every trial type. The first placement after an event took significantly longer than the placement on the event trial, after oddballs (t+1 − t0 = 0.038 log units, SE = 0.009, t(140) = 4.19, p < .001) and after transitions (0.045, SE = 0.012, t(374) = 3.82, p < .001). After transitions, the second placement was again significantly shorter than the first (t+2 − t+1 = −0.035, t(508) = −3.26, p = .001) and no longer differed from t0 (0.010, p = .39). After oddballs, the second placement did not differ significantly from the first (−0.015, p = .083) and remained longer than t0 (0.023, t(171) = 2.64, p = .009), so that at t+2 placements after transitions were shorter than after oddballs (−0.024, t(5289) = −2.26, p = .024); the event type × trial interaction as a whole was not significant (F(2, 3731) = 1.24, p = .29). No term involving condition was significant (condition × trial F(4, 95.6) = 0.28, p = .89; condition × event type × trial F(4, 3731) = 0.83, p = .51), and none of the planned contrasts of the changes between trials (all p ≥ .22).

With the amount of placement work as covariate, the increase from t0 to t+1 was about half as large and remained significant (oddballs, 0.021, p = .017; transitions, 0.027, p = .020), the decrease from t+1 to t+2 after transitions remained (−0.026, p = .016), and the longer placement at t+2 than at t0 after oddballs was no longer significant (0.012, p = .19). Without time-outs, the estimates were similar to those of the primary model (t+1 − t0, 0.035 and 0.037; oddballs, t+2 − t0, 0.026, p = .002). Relative to regular trials, the event trials themselves were placed slightly faster, and the first placements after the event slightly slower (
Figure 2

Classified by strategy at t+1, placements with nets on both directions took significantly longer than placements at the t0 position (0.065 log units, t(1977) = 3.50, p < .001), and followed placements were slightly shorter (−0.027, p = .039). With the number of positions used and the shift as covariates, the difference for nets on both directions disappeared (−0.005, p = .82), and followed placements were significantly shorter than stays (−0.077, t(1951) = −3.36, p < .001). The longer duration of placements on both directions thus reflects the larger number of positions to be filled, whereas a complete move to the new direction was faster than its placement work would imply.
Questionnaire scores and placement duration

In the across-condition model with the questionnaire (P1), no questionnaire term was significant after correction (questionnaire main effects, all q ≥ .43; trial × questionnaire, smallest p = .073 for OCI and p = .094 for STICSA state anxiety; event type × trial × questionnaire, all p ≥ .35, all q ≥ .99). Of the simple contrasts of the questionnaire slopes, the increase of the duration from t0 to t+1 after oddballs was significantly larger with higher STICSA state anxiety (difference of the slopes = 0.025 log units per SD, SE = 0.009, t(143) = 2.84, p = .005; Benjamini–Hochberg across the five questionnaires for this contrast, q = .025) and OCI scores (0.022, SE = 0.009, t(140) = 2.43, p = .016, q = .041), but not significantly with STICSA trait anxiety (0.017, p = .067), BDI (0.015, p = .11) or IU scores (0.010, p = .27). After transitions, the corresponding slopes had the same sign and were not significant (STICSA state 0.010, OCI 0.016, all p ≥ .13). Because the event type × trial × questionnaire interaction was not significant, these contrasts do not show that the questionnaire association differs between oddballs and transitions. The general speed of placement on regular trials was not associated with any questionnaire (participant-level regressions with condition, all p ≥ .15, all q ≥ .46).
Descriptively (
Figure 3

), participants with STICSA state scores above the median (above 30; n = 41) placed the nets 5.1 % longer at t+1 than at t0 after oddballs (mean 4.38 s versus 4.60 s), and participants at or below the median (n = 43) 2.7 % longer (4.26 versus 4.38 s); 78 % and 67 % of them, respectively, took longer at t+1 than at t0 on average. By tertile of the STICSA state score, the increase was 1.2 %, 5.0 % and 5.5 %. For OCI, the increase was 2.7 % at or below the median (9.5; n = 42) and 5.1 % above it (n = 42), and 1.7 %, 4.3 % and 5.7 % by tertile; 62 % and 83 % of the participants took longer at t+1. The participant-level Spearman correlations of the increase with the questionnaire scores were small (STICSA state ρ = .18, p = .11; OCI ρ = .21, p = .062; STICSA trait .11, BDI .13, IU .07). After transitions, the increase was 4.7 % and 4.3 % below and above the median of STICSA state anxiety and 2.7 % and 6.4 % below and above the median of OCI (ρ = .11 and .18, p ≥ .10).

children.alt: Change of the placement duration from the event trial (t0) to the first placement after the event (t+1), per participant (mean over the participant’s events; percent), against the five questionnaire scores, after oddballs (top) and transitions (bottom). Lines are least-squares fits.

Higher state anxiety and OCI scores thus went with a somewhat larger slowing of the first placement after a displaced attack, of about 2.5 % of the duration per SD, but the trial-level model did not distinguish this slowing between oddballs and transitions, and the correlation at the level of participants was small.
